title: Four Vashon artists give old fabrics new life at Studio V - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber
content: Clockwise from left, Roxy Hathaway, Nancy Scott-Wienker, Dorothy Dunnicliff and Sally Shivers gather around a worktable at Studio V, where they make and sell their work. (Phil Clapham Photo) A model wears an orange and blue silk gown by Studio V artist Dorothy Dunnicliff. (Phil Clapham Photo) Tucked away in the center of town, on the back deck behind Herban Bloom, is Studio V, which serves as both the showroom and workspace of four textile or fabric artists who have worked together for many years. First, how does one pronounce the name of the store — is it “Studio Five” (as in the Roman numeral) or “Studio Vee”? The short answer is, well, it could be either. Originally it was the former, back when the four artists were assisted by Dorothy Dunnicliff’s husband Jeff. But after he moved on to do other things and five became four, they decided that “V” might as well stand for “Vashon,” and duly kept the name. Collectively, the four have many decades of experience, both living on the island and producing clothing and a wide variety of accessories. Nancy Scott-Wienker has the longest tenure on Vashon. She arrived here from eastern Oregon in 1972, coming to work for friends who operated a candle factory on the island. She works entirely with repurposed materials and makes a multiplicity of artistic products — gloves, Japanese market bags, capes, ponchos, handbags and tablecloths. Many of her items are crafted from Japanese obi material. Roxy Hathaway (whose father was an Air Force pilot) is next in the timeline. “I came here 40-odd years ago,” she says. Why? She laughs. “I was a hippie in Seattle. I was going to different people’s parties, and they kept saying, ‘You should go to Vashon — you’d love it.’ So I came out here and saw a house with the word NIRVANA carved out of driftwood above the door, and that was it — I knew this was the place for me.” She adds that she almost immediately rented a house for $110 a month “and then figured I’d better get a job here to pay for it.” At the studio, Hathaway enhances jean jackets and denim with different designs and makes caps from repurposed cashmere. “I call it ‘upscaling,’” she says — a concept which is a theme for all the artists at Studio V. Dorothy Dunnicliff was originally from California but bounced around between there and Washington state (including Whidbey Island and Kent) before settling on Vashon in 1988. She operated a store here called Dova Silks for a number of years, originally with the late Valerie Spear, who taught her how to dye silk. Dunnicliff is known for producing beautifully dyed, elegant dresses and other clothing (“She’s a genius,” commented Nancy Scott-Wienker). The fourth artist at Studio V is Sally Shivers, who came to Vashon 36 years ago. Born in Maryland, she was an Air Force brat who moved around a lot. Her father worked at the Pentagon. Her husband is a pilot, and they moved to Vashon for the simple reason that “we had a plane, and Vashon had an airport.” Shivers designs in silk (including leftover materials from Dunnicliff’s garments), cotton, linens, Tencel and wool — tops, jackets and dresses with embellishments and unusual combinations. “Everything gets used here,” she notes. She’s a seamstress and a pattern maker as well as a designer, and her family has a long history of sewing. “My mother made all her own clothes,” she says, “and my grandmother worked sewing machines for Sears in Memphis, Tennessee.” She herself has been in the business of sewing apparel for more than 50 years. “Roxy and I both had mothers who modeled,” she adds, “and their style influenced us.” Studio V has been operating for 16 years, but the women have known each other for much longer. They did work together and realized it just made sense to operate a store together. During its existence, Studio V has put on a number of fashion shows at Open Space and other venues, with the intention of featuring local artists and designers. Unusually, the store is also a workspace. As Scott-Wienker says, “Everything you see is made or modified here. Who else sews all their stuff right there in their shop?” She comments, “I call it ‘slow fashion’ — everything we sell is handmade and one of a kind.” And, she notes, “It’s a great place to shop for a gift for a woman!” (Plus, the store sells gift certificates.) Hathaway adds, “If I was a woman going to a wedding, and I wanted to make sure no one there looks like me, I’d come here.” Like all artists who produce unique items, there is a beauty in the creative process, which often doesn’t turn out quite how you’d imagined. Nancy Scott-Wienker sums it up well. “You have a concept of what you want to do,” she says. “But the piece makes its own way into what it wants to become.” Studio V is at 17600 Vashon Highway S., but not actually on the highway. Walk through the corridor past Swiftwater Gallery and find them on the back deck. “I think a lot of people don’t realize where we are,” says Shivers. “Unfortunately,” she laughs, “the location makes us a bit of a hidden gem.” The studio is usually open Thursday through Saturday, from noon to 4 p.m., or by appointment. Studio V will also be included on the VIVA Holiday Arts Tour from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on the first two weekends of December. Phil Clapham is a retired whale biologist and writer who lives on Maury Island. Thank you for reading the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber.Subscribe to get Unlimited Access to our website.

title: Xavier v. Cleveland State: Preview and keys to the game - Banners On The Parkway
content: I’ve been to a lot of funerals. I don’t think it’s standard deviations above to norm for a person my age, but it’s a large enough number that I’ve got a decent feel for the different ways they can go. For instance, my grandfather passed away last year. He was a good dude who lived a long and full life, and we got together and ate food, told stories, and enjoyed reminiscing about the joy he brought over something on the order of eight decades of life. On the other end of the spectrum are the kind of morose, somber events that accompany tragedy. Rather than belabor that point with examples, I’ll just note that I was in the building the last time Xavier played Cleveland State. There was the overbearing feeling that the program was staggering to some listless future under Travis Steele, or perhaps without him. The speculation that he was coaching his last home game at Cintas was accompanied by rumors that Cleveland State head coach Dennis Gates might be the next head man at Xavier. The game was conducted as almost the backdrop to this drama. The Muskies won despite the visitors having the ball with a chance to tie or take the lead with under a minute left. Travis Steele was fired the next day. Add Banners On The Parkway as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. Fast forward four and a half years and both programs have hired new head coaches twice since that game. CSU is dire, having won two games over KenPom rating aggregating to 673 by a total of a single basket. By contrast, the vibes could not be more immaculate for the Muskies. They proved to be more than flat track bullies in a relentless 18-point beatdown of Mississippi State. Now they’re back home for one more cupcake before a brutal stretch of 4 KenPom top-50 opponents in 5 games. Things have changed significantly since the last time these two teams met. It would take an unforeseeable catastrophe for the game to be as close as it was then. Modern basketball analysis identifies four factors at each end of the court that correlate strongly with success, and Cleveland State is solid in two of those on the defensive end. They’re just outside the top 50 with an OReb% allowed of just 25.8%. They’re even better in the realm of defensive free throw rate, currently sitting 16th in the country in that metric. Unfortunately, those admirable efforts are entirely undercut by abysmal performances in forcing turnover and EFG% allowed, both of which they’re outside the top 350 in. You’ll get your shots up against these guys, and they’ll be good ones. So good that they’re 355th nationally in AdjD. They’re also awful on offense, but it pales in comparison to how bad they are on defense. They’re 251st in the nation in TO%, coughing it up on almost 20% of their trips down the floor. They’re a bad shooting team, especially from behind the arc, and they don’t get to the glass or the line very well. They play incredibly slowly; it’s just kind of an ugly brand of basketball. All of this is exacerbated by roster construction. They’re tied for last in the country in minutes continuity at 0.0%; not a single minute came back from last year. They’re also incredibly young, ranking 347th in the nation in experience. It’s tough sledding pretty much the whole way for Cleveland State so far. -What’s up with Big Fil? Borovicanin was a bright spot in a tough season last year for the Muskies. This year, his shooting numbers are down from behind the arc and at the line, he’s not rebounding as well, and his turnover rate is way up. If this is just a slow start while he finds his place in the new look roster, it’s all good. He’s running out of runway before things get tough though; some signs of life from the senior point forward would be welcome. -Did Tru Washington break out against Mississippi State? The senior guard had been warming slowly to life in a Xavier uniform, but he took a huge leap forward with 21/8/4 last time out. He has the kind of offensive talent that can take over a game, and it was on full display against the Bulldogs. Xavier lost more than 75% of their minutes from last year’s team; Washington stepping up as The Guy would be a huge boon to this iteration of the Muskies. -Is there any danger here? Cleveland State has played one game against a high-major opponent, their season opener against Missouri. In that game, they surrendered runs of 18-2, 15-2, and 10-0 in the first half and 12-2 out of halftime en route to losing 111-50. Theoretically, no D1 opponent can be entirely overlooked, but the Vikings have given every indication that they don’t belong on the same court as Xavier this year. -Dominate tempo. Cleveland State likes to play slowly, and no wonder. It’s hard to be enthusiastic about maximizing chances to do something poorly. Xavier, on the other hand, is third in the nation in adjusted tempo. More possessions equal more opportunities for talent to shine through, and X has the advantage there in spades. Turning this thing into a track meet favors the home team. -Keep the pressure high on the ballhandlers. The Vikings’ ball security is poor, and that starts with the guards. Their primary ballhandlers have all struggled with turnovers this year, and Xavier can feast on turning defense into offense by forcing them into tough positions. CSU is prone to surrendering big runs, and those can happen in the blink of an eye once turnovers start piling up. -Fine tune. Xavier’s next three games after this one are against top-50, high-major opponents, and two of them are away from home. The time to play in the margin for error is rapidly diminishing. Whatever rough edges need sanded smooth have to be handled posthaste; it gets a lot more real from here. The season opens with a visit from the Mountaineers of the newly rebranded Metro Conference. title: After midseason forfeit, La Jolla Country Day rallies to reach Div. V quarterfinals - Times of San Diego
content: LA JOLLA – The injuries kept mounting. At one point, La Jolla Country Day didn’t have enough healthy players to take the field. The Torreys nevertheless reached the CIF-San Diego Section Div. V quarterfinals before their season ended Friday night with a 34-13 loss to Olympian. The severity of the injuries became clear in October, when La Jolla Country Day forfeited its Oct. 8 game against undefeated county powerhouse Santa Fe Christian rather than risk putting an undermanned team on the field. The Torreys had just 34 players on their roster, including 14 freshmen. Following a 35-0 loss to Bishop’s and a bye week, injuries left them without enough healthy players to compete safely, head coach Carmy Cesaire said. “It was tough because we want to coach games, play games and compete. That’s football. But I just couldn’t see anybody else get hurt,” Cesaire said. “I told the parents I wasn’t going to put the kids in that position, where we’d have to put someone out there who had never played before. We weren’t going to throw 14-year-olds to the dogs.” The players understood the decision, Cesaire said, even though it meant giving up a chance to compete. “We would have played that game 100 times out of 100 if we could,” he said. “I think the young guys were probably a little bit relieved. It was a chance to breathe, get healthy and get back into it.” “Forfeiting on a team is never a mindset you have planned in advance as a team,” said Marvin Jones III, a wide receiver who moved to quarterback amid the injuries. “We were low on guys and didn’t want to risk further injuries on the team that could potentially affect our outcome of the season moving forward. “So, it’s not a matter of we were not capable of playing SFC, more that we were putting the team first and preparing for what is best for the team and what was going to happen in the long run.” No position was hit harder than quarterback. The Torreys went through four quarterbacks in a Week 4 loss to La Jolla High. Starter Will Bertrand, who threw 10 touchdowns in the team’s first three games, suffered a season-ending broken leg early in the game. Jones took over before an MCL injury sidelined him for several weeks. Rocco Taccone stepped in next, but an AC joint injury forced the Torreys to turn to sophomore Jaydon Turman. La Jolla Country Day lost six offensive starters through the first six weeks, forcing players into unfamiliar roles and the coaching staff to simplify its offense. We have lost a ton of people for a significant amount of time.” “We’ve kept it real simple these last few weeks. You don’t motion as much, you stick to a couple of formations and get good at a couple of plays,” Cesaire said. “We’ve focused on fundamentals and techniques. When you lose one guy, you’re losing three guys for us — an offensive player, a defensive player and a special teams guy. It was cool to see some of the young guys, especially sophomores and juniors, step up and take on different roles.” Senior Owen Dorros became one of the Torreys’ most versatile players, contributing at wide receiver, running back and kicker. After years of playing soccer, Dorros began playing tackle football in eighth grade. His soccer background led coaches to put him at kicker, but he continued working at receiver, his preferred position. Dorros finished the season with 316 rushing yards and three touchdowns on 53 carries, while catching 52 passes for 736 yards and nine touchdowns. He also made all 27 of his extra-point attempts and converted three of five field-goal attempts, including a season-long 44-yarder. “He got off to a hot start receiving-wise before my injury, but he has continued to make plays as both a receiver and running back, doing whatever the team needs him to,” Bertrand said. Dorros said losing both the starting and backup quarterbacks against La Jolla affected team morale but reinforced the need to find his own role. “Losing our starting and backup quarterback against La Jolla definitely hurt team morale a lot,” Dorros said. “I was told to play kicker and fell in love with it while continuing to work on my skills at receiver until I’d get the opportunity to play. “I think kicking is what has got me so far throughout my high school football career because it always felt like there was a reason I was on the team, even when my true passion was getting the ball out at receiver. I knew from the get-go I would have to find a place on the team.” After the bye and forfeit, the Torreys returned Oct. 16 against Coastal Academy with Jones back at quarterback. He completed 17 of 21 passes for two touchdowns and rushed for two more in a 49-14 home win. Jones’ return gave the Torreys stability after weeks of uncertainty. Cesaire said the senior’s commitment to the quarterback position had grown since the previous season. “When he started coming back and started practicing, you could just see the whole vibe of the team changed, the energy changed,” Cesaire said. “Last year, I think he was just an athlete back there. If he didn’t like it, he was gone. And then he was like, ‘I’m going to be a pocket passer. I’m going to stand in there.
